places.history: DOCUMENTED: Gripsholms Värdshus at Kyrkogatan 1, Mariefred (Södermanland), beside Gripsholm Castle on Lake Mälaren. In the early 1600s Mariefred had no dedicated coaching inn; burghers were obliged to lodge travellers, and court servants of Charles IX — who frequently resided at Gripsholm — were housed without payment as a form of tax. Burgher protests in 1609 led to a royal letter of privilege dated 13 February 1609 naming the first innkeeper, Jocim (Joachim) Smock from Germany, previously a Stockholm tavern keeper; the Smock Room still commemorates him. The site lies on land of the former Carthusian monastery Pax Mariae (Mary's Peace), dissolved mid-1520s, which gave Mariefred its name; during 1980s renovations monastic remains were found and some are preserved in the wine cellar. Castle accounts mention a gästgivare building as early as 1592, but the exact first inn location is uncertain; the present plot (gård 7–8, kvarteret Källaren) was built by at least 1613. The business later operated under names including Stadshotellet and Stadskällaren. The current main building dates largely to the mid-18th century; after a 1957 lightning fire at a Lottenlund site that briefly carried the Gripsholms värdshus name, the Mariefred inn was extensively restored and reopened in 1989 with a 12-metre extension housing royal suites and parquet floors modelled on Swedish castle originals. Across four centuries the inn has hosted royalty, noble families, merchants, military officers and travellers, surviving wars, epidemics and ownership changes while remaining one of Sweden's oldest operating inns. Nearby Gripsholm Castle (Gustav Vasa foundation; Charles IX renovation; later royal residence, prison and State Portrait Collection) shares the same royal-civic landscape. DARK HISTORY (documented context, not paranormal claims): centuries of arrivals and departures imply ordinary deaths from age, illness and accident among guests and staff; Mariefred and Södermanland endured plague periods, wartime hardship and castle dramas that form the emotional backdrop of the place — Haunted Sweden does not invent specific hauntings from these facts alone.
places.legend: FOLKLORE & WITNESS REPORTS (not scientifically verified): Guests and staff for many decades describe footsteps in empty corridors, unexplained voices, doors opening or closing by themselves, cold spots, a sense of being watched, and occasional sightings of figures in grey-brown monastic habits with dark hoods — commonly linked in local tradition to Carthusian monks of Pax Mariae rather than to named historical individuals. Rooms 115 and 210 are most frequently cited; some guests report waking to a duvet moving as if tucked in, described as a gentle rather than hostile presence. The wine cellar is repeatedly named in staff stories (shadows, odd sounds, atmosphere). Media and paranormal sites (e.g. Myling and Swedish ghost lists) also weave castle lore into the Mariefred picture — including older anecdotes of moving door handles in castle wings — but Haunted Sweden treats castle reports as related regional folklore, not proof of activity at the inn. SPECIAL AREAS: historic guest rooms (original detailing + unexplained-experience reports); old corridors (footsteps, heavy atmosphere after midnight); restaurant and dining rooms (centuries as a gathering place); courtyard with views toward Gripsholm Castle. ATMOSPHERE: traditional Swedish inn, wooden interiors, antiques, candlelit dining, quiet post-midnight corridors, charming Mariefred streets — strongest in autumn, winter darkness and rain. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: overnight stay; EVP in historic corridors; night photography; staff interviews; compare guest reports; night walk between inn and castle; contrast inn legends with castle legends. BEST CONDITIONS: overnight, autumn evenings, winter dark, rain, quiet weekdays. Separate DOCUMENTED history (privileges 1609, Smock, monastery ground, building phases) from WITNESS REPORTS and FOLKLORE above.

places.history: DOCUMENTED: Home Hotel Bilan occupies Karlbergsgatan 3, Karlstad (Värmland) — the former Länscellfängelset i Karlstad (later Straffängelset i Karlstad), opened 1847 among Sweden's early cellular prisons after the 1844 riksdag reform. From 1911 the larger county cellular prisons including Karlstad were redesignated straffängelse. Kriminalvården left the building in 1968. The property later also served psychiatric care before hotel conversion; Hotell Bilan opened after rebuilding in 1985 (today Home Hotel Bilan / Strawberry). Much original prison character remains: corridor layout, thick stone walls, iron doors, cell volumes adapted as guest rooms, and a small prison museum in the basement. Notable documented inmates include Anders Lindbäck (the Silbodal priest), among others recorded in prison history. places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Torpa Stenhus beside Lake Åsunden near Länghem is one of Sweden's best-preserved medieval stone castles — begun around 1470 by councillor Arvid Knutsson as a fortified stronghold, expanded in the 1500s–1600s, and held by the Stenbock family through inheritance for centuries without commercial sale. In 1552 Gustav Vasa took his third wife, Katarina Stenbock, from Torpa. Visitors come for Renaissance interiors, the Great Hall, baroque chapel and lakeside setting — and for western Sweden's most famous castle ghost lore: the Grey Lady in the upper halls, the Walled-In Girl of plague folklore, and Little Gustav, said to have drowned in a well aged three. Guides tell the stories freely; Haunted Sweden keeps documented building and dynastic history clearly separate from legend and visitor reports of footsteps, cold spots and shadow figures. places.history: DOCUMENTED: Torpa Stenhus (Torpa Gård, Länghem, Tranemo municipality, Västra Götaland / Västergötland) stands west of Lake Åsunden. The first stone house was built around 1470 by riksråd Arvid Knutsson as a defensive and trading stronghold amid Danish war threats and local unrest; a parchment letter of 9 February 1513 from Vadstena is among the earliest archival mentions of the stone house at Torpa. Around mid-1500s the stair tower was added; late-1500s works raised roofs, added a fourth storey and decorated halls. Torpa became the principal stamgods of the Stenbock family and has never been sold commercially — inheritance on male or female lines from the medieval builders to the present owners. In 1552, after visiting Torpa, Gustav Vasa chose Katarina Stenbock (daughter of Gustav Olofsson Stenbock and Brita Leijonhufvud) as his third wife — she was collected/taken from Torpa into royal marriage. Early 1600s mark a golden age; Gustav Otto Stenbock later preferred a timber residence for comfort while using the stone house for representation. The castle chapel in Caroline baroque was completed for consecration in 1699 under Christina Katarina de la Gardie after Gustav Otto's death. Surviving fabric includes massive medieval walls, Renaissance Great Hall (riddarsalen), thick oak doors, stair tower and chapel — among Sweden's best-preserved manor castles of the type. DARK HISTORY (documented context, not hauntings): medieval fortification and warfare climate, noble politics, centuries of ordinary illness and death in an isolated lakeside stronghold, and family tragedies recorded in genealogy and local history form the emotional backdrop — Haunted Sweden does not treat folklore deaths as proven events.
places.legend: FOLKLORE (castle tradition / official ghost pages — not documented history): THE GREY LADY (Gråa frun / Grå damen): Said to be a lord's daughter who loved a Danish prisoner her father had brought home; when he killed the captive she died of grief and still wanders the halls as a silent woman in grey, often linked to upper floors after dark — one of Torpa's oldest surviving ghost traditions. THE WALLED-IN GIRL (Den inmurade flickan): Legend of a knight's daughter bricked up alive after returning from Denmark and mentioning plague on her ship; her father feared contagion. Versions vary (sister confided in, night awakening, masons, chair by a window). She is said to wander seeking freedom — clearly folklore, not proven burial. LITTLE GUSTAV (Lille Gustav Stenbock): Local legend that young Gustav, first-born son of Gustaf Otto Stenbock, drowned in a well at age three; visitors (especially women, in site lore) report a pale boy in historic clothing. RELATED FOLKLORE also names white horses before an owner's death and Greve Gustaf Otto Stenbock (portrait / midnight calling tale) — secondary to the three focus legends above. WITNESS REPORTS & GUIDES (unverified): footsteps in empty corridors, doors opening unexpectedly, shadow figures, cold spots, feeling watched — shared by guides, visitors and staff in haunted-castle lists. SPECIAL AREAS: Great Hall; upper floors (Grey Lady); corridors; former well area (Little Gustav); exterior courtyard after sunset. ATMOSPHERE: stone walls, Renaissance hall, ancient stairs, oak doors, Åsunden views, fog on the grounds. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: evening visit with permission; Grey Lady / Walled-In Girl / Little Gustav story mapping vs archives; EVP in Great Hall; castle after dark only when allowed. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn evenings, heavy fog, winter darkness, rain, blue hour. Separate DOCUMENTED history from FOLKLORE above.
places.safetyNote: Privately owned historic castle — visit only via official openings, guided tours and booked events (torpastenhus.se). Stay on permitted paths; do not enter closed floors, climb walls or trespass after hours. Respect staff, other visitors and photography rules. Night investigation only with explicit permission.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Ett av Sveriges finaste medeltida stenhus vid Åsunden — Stenbock-arv, Gustav Vasas Katarina och legendariska spöken som Gråa frun.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Torpa Stenhus vid sjön Åsunden, Länghem (Tranemo, Västra Götaland). Första stenhuset ca 1470 av riksrådet Arvid Knutsson som försvars- och handelsborg; omnämnt i pergamentbrev 9 februari 1513. Trapptorn och tillbyggnader 1500–1600-tal; renässansriddarsal; slottskapell invigt 1699. Stenbockarnas stamgods — aldrig sålt, endast ärvt. 1552 hämtade Gustav Vasa sin tredje hustru Katarina Stenbock från Torpa. Mörk historia som kontext: medeltida krigshot, adelspolitik, sjukdom och familjetragedier — inte automatiska spökbevis.
places.legendSv: FOLKLORE (ej dokumenterad historia): GRÅA FRUN — herrdotter som älskade en dansk fånge; vandrar i grått, ofta övre våningar. DEN INMURADE FLICKAN — riddardotter inmurad levande efter pestoro från Danmark; söker frihet — legend. LILLE GUSTAV STENBOCK — drunknade i brunnen som treåring enligt sägen; blek pojke i gamla kläder. VITTNESMÅL: fotsteg, dörrar, skuggor, köld — guider och besökare. Håll isär från dokumenterad byggnads- och ätteshistoria.
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummarySv: Torpa Stenhus vid Åsunden är ett av Sveriges bäst bevarade medeltida stenhus — uppfört ca 1470, Stenbockarnas stamgods, och platsen där Gustav Vasa 1552 hämtade Katarina Stenbock. Hit kommer besökare för renässanssalar och för västra Sveriges mest kända slottsspöken: Gråa frun, den inmurade flickan och lille Gustav. Haunted Sweden skiljer dokumenterad historia från folklore. Boka officiella visningar; höstdimma och blåtimme gör Torpa till en flaggskeppsdestination.
places.safetyNoteSv: Privatägt historiskt slott – besök endast via officiella öppningar, guidade visningar och bokade evenemang. Håll dig till tillåtna stigar; gå inte in på stängda våningar, klättra inte på murar eller trespassera efter stängning. Respektera personal, besökare och fotoregler. Nattutredning endast med uttryckligt tillstånd.
